title: Building a Proof Argument — GPS Step 5

subChunks.title: Building a Proof Argument — GPS Step 5

storyBeats.txt: The Genealogical Proof Standard has five steps, Theodora said. Most researchers manage the first four tolerably. The fifth is where the work becomes writing — and that is where most researchers stop.

GPS Step 5 is the soundly reasoned, coherently written conclusion. For simple conclusions — proved directly by a single original source — it can be as brief as a sentence. But for complex conclusions, the ones that require assembling multiple pieces of indirect and negative evidence, it becomes a proof argument.

A proof argument is a formal piece of genealogical writing. It presents the research question, surveys the relevant records, analyses the evidence, resolves any conflicts, and reaches a stated conclusion. It is, essentially, a short academic paper.

The test for a proof argument is simple: could a competent genealogist, reading only what you have written, follow your reasoning and either agree with your conclusion or identify exactly where they disagree? If yes, you have written a proof argument. If no — you have written a story.

subChunks.hookHtml:
The Genealogical Proof Standard's fifth element — a 'soundly reasoned, coherently written conclusion' — is the culmination of everything that precedes it. Without this final step, even the most thorough research remains a private collection of notes rather than a communicable, verifiable finding.

In practice, this element takes one of three forms: a proof statement (a single sentence or paragraph for simple conclusions directly supported by evidence); a proof summary (a short essay drawing together multiple evidences); or a proof argument (a fully developed, footnoted argument for complex conclusions that depend on indirect and negative evidence and require resolution of conflicts). Understanding when each form is appropriate, and how to write it, is an essential professional skill.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
When Is a Proof Argument Required?

A proof argument is required when no single source directly proves the conclusion. This situation arises when: all relevant sources are indirect or negative; sources conflict and the conflict must be resolved in writing; the conclusion derives from DNA evidence correlated with documentary evidence; or the conclusion contradicts a previously published or accepted finding and must explicitly rebut it.

A proof statement suffices when a single, reliable, original source directly proves the fact in question and no conflicting evidence exists. A proof summary is intermediate — multiple sources directly prove the conclusion with minimal conflict.

Structure of a Proof Argument

A well-constructed proof argument has four sections:

  1. Research question: A precise statement of what is being proved. 'Who were the parents of John Smith baptised at St Mary's, Coventry, in 1823?' is better than 'John Smith's family'. The question defines the scope.
  2. Survey of relevant records: What record types could provide evidence? Which survive and have been searched? Which do not survive (or were never created)? This section establishes that the research has been reasonably exhaustive — GPS Step 1.
  3. Analysis of evidence: Each piece of evidence is classified (source, information, evidence type) and its probative value assessed. Indirect and negative evidence is explicitly identified as such. Conflicting evidence is acknowledged — not ignored.
  4. Conclusion: A stated finding, with the evidential basis summarised: 'The preponderance of evidence indicates that…' or 'The available evidence establishes with reasonable confidence that…'. Limitations are acknowledged.

Footnote Practice

Every factual assertion in a proof argument must be supported by a footnote citing the specific source used. Elizabeth Shown Mills's Evidence Explained provides citation templates for virtually every genealogical source type. Key principles: cite the specific record, not just the database; give the repository and record identifier; note the date accessed for online sources. Vague citations ('Ancestry.com — birth certificate') are not acceptable in professional work.

Resolving Conflicting Evidence in the Argument

When sources conflict, the proof argument must explicitly state the conflict and explain why one interpretation is preferred. Arguments for resolution may include: one source is more reliable (original vs. derivative; primary vs. secondary information); one source was created closer in time to the event; one source is consistent with multiple corroborating pieces of evidence while the other stands alone; one source's informant had better knowledge than the other's.

Example: Two census entries give a woman's birth year as 1837 and 1845 respectively. Her baptism register entry (1839) resolves the conflict — the baptism is an original source with primary information, created closest in time to the event. The proof argument explicitly notes both census discrepancies, cites the baptism as the controlling source, and acknowledges that the census ages are unreliable for this individual.

The Proof Argument vs. the Narrative

A family history narrative tells the story of a family. A proof argument proves a specific genealogical conclusion. They are different genres. The proof argument is analytical and argumentative; it aims to establish facts. The narrative is synthetic and communicative; it aims to bring those facts to life. A published family history will contain both — narratives built on foundations of previously constructed proof arguments.

Board for Certification of Genealogists (BCG) applicants must submit a portfolio including at least one proof argument, demonstrating competence in GPS-compliant written analysis. The National Genealogical Society Quarterly (NGSQ) publishes peer-reviewed proof arguments and is the primary venue for model examples.

Common Failures in Proof Arguments

  • Stating a conclusion first and then selecting only supporting evidence — confirmation bias in written form.
  • Treating a derivative source (index entry, transcription) as equivalent to the original.
  • Acknowledging no limitations or conflicts when some clearly exist.
  • Using imprecise language ('probably', 'likely') without explaining the basis for the probabilistic assessment.
  • Failing to cite the specific records searched to establish negative evidence.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what a genealogical proof argument is and why it is different from just telling a story about your family.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: You are constructing a proof argument to answer the question: 'Was Martha Rowe (born c.1818, Lincolnshire) the same person as the Martha Rowe who married Thomas Baines in 1841 at Boston, Lincolnshire?' Evidence: (1) 1841 census shows Martha Baines, age 20, born Lincolnshire, living with Thomas Baines; (2) 1851 census shows Martha Baines, age 32, born Spalding, Lincolnshire; (3) GRO marriage register entry 1841: Martha Rowe married Thomas Baines, Boston; both signed with a mark; (4) baptism register at Spalding parish church: Martha Rowe baptised 14 March 1818, daughter of John and Ann Rowe; (5) no other Martha Rowe baptism found in Lincolnshire 1815–1825. Draft the research question, evidence survey, and a brief evidence analysis for this proof argument.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
Research question: Can the Martha Rowe baptised at Spalding, Lincolnshire in 1818 be identified as the Martha Rowe who married Thomas Baines at Boston, Lincolnshire in 1841?

Evidence survey: Records consulted include: GRO marriage index and register entry; Lincolnshire parish baptism registers via Ancestry and FindMyPast; 1841 and 1851 census returns; Lincolnshire county history for geographic context. The baptism register for Spalding survives complete for 1800–1850 (confirmed by FindMyPast coverage indicator). No other Martha Rowe baptism was found in Lincolnshire 1815–1825.

Evidence analysis:

(1) The 1841 marriage entry provides direct evidence that a Martha Rowe married Thomas Baines at Boston in 1841. Both parties signed with marks — consistent with limited literacy, common in agricultural labourers of this period.

(2) The 1841 census entry: the age of 20 (censuses typically rounded to nearest 5) is consistent with a birth year of 1818–1823. Secondary information; indirect evidence of approximate age.

(3) The 1851 census entry: age 32 implies birth year c.1819, consistent with the 1818 baptism. 'Born Spalding' is more specific than the 1841 entry and is consistent with the Spalding baptism — though secondary information from the wife's own testimony, so has some weight as self-reported evidence.

(4) The baptism entry is direct, primary evidence that a Martha Rowe was born to John and Ann Rowe at Spalding in 1818.

(5) Negative evidence: no other Martha Rowe baptism in Lincolnshire 1815–1825. This eliminates alternative candidates and strengthens the identification.

Preliminary conclusion: The preponderance of evidence establishes that the Martha Rowe baptised at Spalding in 1818 is almost certainly the Martha Rowe who married Thomas Baines in 1841. The 1851 census's specific birthplace 'Spalding' is the key corroborating detail; the absence of any other candidate in the county strengthens the conclusion further.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Write a proof argument answering the following question: 'Was William Cooper (died 1872 in Staffordshire) the father of James Cooper baptised at Wolverhampton in 1843?' You have the following evidence: (1) James Cooper's death certificate (1921) names his father as 'William Cooper, ironworker'; (2) 1851 census: William Cooper, age 38, ironworker, born Wolverhampton, with son James age 8; (3) 1871 census: William Cooper, age 58, retired ironworker, no children in household; (4) William Cooper death certificate 1872: age 59, ironworker; (5) baptism register, St Peter's Wolverhampton, 1843: James Cooper, son of William and Mary Cooper. No other William Cooper ironworker appears in Wolverhampton in the 1851 or 1861 census.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Research question: Was William Cooper, ironworker, who died in Staffordshire in 1872, the father of James Cooper baptised at St Peter's, Wolverhampton in 1843?

Survey of relevant records: Evidence considered includes: James Cooper's death certificate (1921); baptism register of St Peter's Wolverhampton (1843); 1851 and 1871 census entries; William Cooper's death certificate (1872). Wolverhampton births index searched for all William Cooper/Cooper baptisms 1811–1816 to identify candidates; only one William Cooper ironworker found in relevant census years.

Evidence analysis:

The 1921 death certificate directly states James Cooper's father was 'William Cooper, ironworker' — but this is secondary information (provided by informant up to 78 years after the stated fact). It establishes that James, at his death, believed or claimed his father was William Cooper, an ironworker.

The 1843 baptism entry directly names James Cooper as son of William and Mary Cooper — this is original, primary evidence for parentage. The 1851 census shows William Cooper, age 38 (b. c.1813), ironworker, with a son James aged 8 (b. c.1843) — ages consistent with both the baptism and William's death certificate (age 59 in 1872, b. c.1813). This is indirect corroborating evidence.

The 1871 census shows William aged 58, consistent with his death certificate, but no children in the household — consistent with adult children having left home by 1871.

The negative evidence (no other William Cooper ironworker found in Wolverhampton) eliminates alternative candidates and strengthens the identification.

Conclusion: The preponderance of evidence establishes with reasonable confidence that William Cooper, ironworker (c.1813–1872), was the father of James Cooper baptised at St Peter's Wolverhampton in 1843. The baptism entry directly links James to a William and Mary Cooper; the 1851 census corroborates both the father's name and James's birth year; the death certificate confirms the father's occupation. No conflicting evidence has been found. The only caveat is that the death certificate information is secondary — but it is corroborated by multiple independent sources.
learningObjectives: Distinguish the three forms of GPS Step 5 conclusion (proof statement, proof summary, proof argument) and identify when each is appropriate.
Construct a proof argument with the four required sections: research question, evidence survey, evidence analysis, and conclusion.
Apply Evidence Explained citation standards to footnoting within a proof argument.
Demonstrate resolution of conflicting evidence within a written proof argument.
commonMistakes: Beginning with a conclusion and selecting only supporting evidence — confirmation bias invalidates the argument.
Omitting the evidence survey section — GPS requires documenting what was searched, including records that yielded no results.
Using vague citations (e.g., 'found on Ancestry') rather than specific source citations with repository and record identifiers.
Conflating a narrative family history with a proof argument — they serve different purposes and follow different conventions.
assessmentCriteria: Proof argument structure is complete: research question, evidence survey, analysis (with explicit source/information/evidence classification), and conclusion.
Conflicting or absent evidence is acknowledged and addressed rather than ignored.
Citations are sufficiently specific for a reader to locate the original sources independently.
Conclusion language accurately reflects the epistemic status ('preponderance of evidence', 'establishes with reasonable confidence') rather than overclaiming certainty.

questions.questionHtml: According to the GPS framework, when is a full proof argument (rather than a proof statement) required?
options: Whenever more than three sources are used in the research
When no single source directly proves the conclusion, or when conflicting evidence must be explicitly resolved
Only when submitting research to a peer-reviewed journal
When the research involves DNA evidence exclusively
questions.correctAnswer: When no single source directly proves the conclusion, or when conflicting evidence must be explicitly resolved
questions.explanationHtml: A proof statement suffices when a single, reliable, original source directly proves the fact with no conflict. A proof argument is required when the conclusion depends on assembling indirect and negative evidence, or when conflicting sources must be explicitly evaluated and resolved in writing.

questions.questionHtml: In a proof argument, you find two census entries giving a woman's birth year as 1842 and 1849. Her baptism register entry records 1845. How should you handle this conflict in the argument?
options: Use the average of the three years (1845.3, rounded to 1845)
Ignore the census ages as unreliable and cite only the baptism

Explicitly acknowledge both census discrepancies, explain why the baptism (original source, primary information, created closest to the event) is the controlling source, and note that census ages are unreliable for this individual
Accept the most recent record (1849 census) as incorporating the most up-to-date information
questions.correctAnswer: Explicitly acknowledge both census discrepancies, explain why the baptism (original source, primary information, created closest to the event) is the controlling source, and note that census ages are unreliable for this individual
questions.explanationHtml: A proof argument must acknowledge conflicts — not suppress them. The resolution must explain why one source is preferred over another, with reference to source quality, information type, and proximity to the event. The baptism is original, primary, and contemporaneous — the strongest type of evidence for birth year.

questions.questionHtml: Which citation is acceptable in a professional proof argument?
options: 'England & Wales Birth Registration, Stoke-on-Trent, September quarter 1847, vol. 17, p. 213; General Register Office, Southport; digital image, Ancestry (www.ancestry.co.uk), accessed 14 April 2025.'
'GRO birth certificate, Stoke-on-Trent, 1847 — confirms name and date.'
'Birth registration indexed on FindMyPast — certificate ordered but not yet received.'
questions.correctAnswer: 'England & Wales Birth Registration, Stoke-on-Trent, September quarter 1847, vol. 17, p. 213; General Register Office, Southport; digital image, Ancestry (www.ancestry.co.uk), accessed 14 April 2025.'
questions.explanationHtml: A professional citation must enable another researcher to locate the exact same record. The acceptable citation provides the record series, registration district, quarter/year, volume and page, repository, and access details. Vague citations like 'found on Ancestry' or 'GRO certificate' do not meet this standard.
